
# Practical Aspects - What can go wrong? {#practical-aspects}

---

## Varying Measurement Intervals

- Discrete-time DSEM models require equidistant measurement intervals 
  - Strength of time-lagged relation depends on the measurement intervals
  - If ignored, AR- and CL effects lack a clear interpretation

- Implemented solution (as in Mplus; Muthén & Muthén, 2017):
  - Missing value insertion strategy (`tinterval`; Asparouhov et al., 2018)
  - Allows approximation of continuous-time lagged effects for specific time intervals

:::{.references}

Asparouhov, T., Hamaker, E. L., & Muthén, B. O. (2018). Dynamic Structural Equation Models. *Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal*, *25(3)*, 359–388. <https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2017.1406803>

Muthén, L. K., & Muthén, B. O. (2017). *Mplus user’s guide* (8th edn). Muthén & Muthén.

:::

. . .

:::{.vspace}
:::  

### How does it work?

## Fixed Sampling Protocol

#### Naive Approach (without correction)

::: {.column width="25%"}

```{r}
options(knitr.kable.NA = 'NA')
set.seed(1)
df = data.frame("ID"   = rep(1, times = 6), 
           "beep" = c(1,2,5,6,7,9),
           "Y"    = sample(size = 6, x = c(1:7), replace = T)
           )
df$Y[4] <- NA

knitr::kable(df, booktabs = TRUE, align = "ccc") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 25) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_classic()

```

:::

::: {.column width="10%"}

:::

::: {.column width="65%"}

```r
mlts_fit(...)
```

```{r, warning = F, message=F, eval = F}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 1.5
```

#### Using `tinterval`

::: {.column width="25%"}

```{r}
set.seed(1)
df = data.frame("ID"   = rep(1, times = 6), 
           "beep" = c(1,2,5,6,7,9),
           "Y"    = sample(size = 6, x = c(1:7), replace = T)
           )
df$Y[4] <- NA

df %>%
  mlts::create_missings(tinterval = 1, id = "ID", time = "beep") %>%
  select(ID, int_time, beep, Y) %>%
  knitr::kable(., booktabs = TRUE, align = "ccccc") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 25) %>%
  row_spec(row = c(3,4,8), color = "darkgreen") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_classic()

```

:::

::: {.column width="10%"}

:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
```r
mlts_fit(..., tinterval = 1, time = "beep")
```
```{r, warning = F, message=F}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 1.5
df %>%
  mlts::create_missings(tinterval = 1, id = "ID", time = "beep") %>%
  mutate(beep_lab = ifelse(is.na(Y), "NA", beep)) %>%
  ggplot(.,aes(x = beep, y = 0.35)) + 
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = int_time-0.25, ymin = 0.1, ymax = 0.6, xmax = int_time+0.25),
              fill = "lightgray", color = "black") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1.25:9.25, y = 0.35, xend = 1.75:9.75, yend = 0.35),
             color = "darkgreen",
    arrow = arrow(type = "closed", length = unit(0.2, units = "cm"))
  ) +
  geom_text(aes(label = beep_lab, 
                x = int_time)) +
  labs(title = "After approximation") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:9) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.7)) +
  theme_classic() + 
  theme(
    axis.line.y = element_blank(),
    axis.title.y = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank()
  )
```

:::



## Random Sampling Protocol

#### Naive Approach (without correction)

::: {.column width="25%"}

```{r}
set.seed(1)
df = data.frame("ID"   = rep(1, times = 6), 
           "time_diff" = as.integer(c(0, runif(n = 5, min = 30, max = 90))),
           "time" = NA,
           "Y"    = sample(size = 6, x = c(1:7), replace = T)
           )


df$time = as.integer(cumsum(df$time_diff))


knitr::kable(df, booktabs = TRUE, align = "ccc") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 25) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_classic()

```

:::

::: {.column width="10%"}

:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
```r
mlts_fit(...)
```

## Application to Empirical Dataset

```{r}
#| include: false

load("./downloaded_data/bolzen_grid.rda")
```


- Running `prepare_bolzen.R` creates a version of the dataset (i.e., `bolzen_grid`) where a new variable is added (`int_time_spaced`)
- `int_time_spaced` can be used as an index variable for `tinterval` 
  - results in 4 additional missing between each `time_window`, and 10 missing values for the overnight period being added  

::::{.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}

```{r}

bolzen_grid %>%
  filter(id == 4 & day_counter < 3) %>%
  select(id, obs_counter, day_counter, time_window, timepoint, time_diff, int_time_spaced, posaff) %>%
  knitr::kable(., align = "c", booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 25) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_classic() %>%
  column_spec(column = 7, color = "darkgreen", bold = T)
```

:::

::: {.column width="5%"}

:::

::: {.column width="30%"}

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: 1-10|6-7|8 
mlts_fit(
    model = model, 
    data = bolzen_grid, 
    id = "id", 
    ts = "posaff",
    time  = "int_time_spaced", 
    tinterval = 1,
    max_NA_seq = 4,
    iter = 2000
    )
```

```{r, eval = F}

### FIT THE MODEL 3 TIMES
model = mlts_model(q = 1)
V1 = mlts_fit(model = model, data = bolzen, id = "id", ts = "posaff",
              iter = 2000)

V2.1 = mlts_fit(model = model, data = bolzen_grid, id = "id", ts = "posaff",
                time  = "int_time_spaced", tinterval = 1, max_NA_seq = 1,
                iter = 2000)
V2.2 = mlts_fit(model = model, data = bolzen_grid, id = "id", ts = "posaff",
                time  = "int_time_spaced", tinterval = 1, max_NA_seq = 2,
                iter = 2000)
V2.3 = mlts_fit(model = model, data = bolzen_grid, id = "id", ts = "posaff",
                time  = "int_time_spaced", tinterval = 1, max_NA_seq = 3,
                iter = 2000)
V2.4 = mlts_fit(model = model, data = bolzen_grid, id = "id", ts = "posaff",
                time  = "int_time_spaced", tinterval = 1, max_NA_seq = 4,
                iter = 2000)
V2.5 = mlts_fit(model = model, data = bolzen_grid, id = "id", ts = "posaff",
                time  = "int_time_spaced", tinterval = 1,
                iter = 2000)

fits = list(
  V1, V2.1, V2.2, V2.3, V2.4, V2.5
)

dir.create("04-practical_aspects")
save(fits, file = "04-practical_aspects/tinterval_fits.Rdata")
```

## Effect of Different Correction Strategies

- Here illustrated for the time series of one individual (`posaff`)

```{r}
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 6

labels = c("No Tinterval", "Tinterval (max_NA_seq = 1)", 
           "Tinterval (max_NA_seq = 2)", "Tinterval (max_NA_seq = 3)",
           "Tinterval (max_NA_seq = 4)", "Tinterval (without restriction)")

load("sections/04-practical_aspects/tinterval_fits.Rdata")

dats = do.call(plyr::rbind.fill,lapply(c(1,2,5,6), function(x){
    
    dat = fits[[x]]$data %>% filter(id == 1)
    dat$Est = labels[x]
    dat %>%
      mutate(row = 1:n())
  }))

ggplot(dats, aes(x = row, y = posaff)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = obs_counter)) +
  geom_line() +
  ggh4x::facet_grid2(rows = vars(Est), strip = ggh4x::strip_split(position = "top")) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    strip.background = element_blank(),
    strip.text = element_text(face = 2,size = 16),
    panel.spacing.y = unit(x = 0.6, units = "cm"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )


```

#### How does this affect estimates derived from the AR(1) model?

## Consequences for Population Parameter Estimates

- Fixed effects

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4

all_pars = do.call(rbind, lapply(1:length(fits), function(x){
  cbind("label" = labels[x], fits[[x]]$pop.pars.summary)
}))

all_pars %>%
  filter(Param %in% c("mu_1", "phi(1)_11", "ln.sigma2_1")) %>% 
  mutate(Param = factor(Param, levels = c("mu_1", "phi(1)_11", "ln.sigma2_1"))) %>%
  ggplot(., aes(x = label, y = mean, color = label)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = `2.5%`, ymax = `97.5%`), width = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(group = Param), alpha = 0.5, color = "darkgrey") +
  facet_wrap(~Param, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(" ", values = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(name = "Greens", n = 9)[4:9]) + 
  labs(y = "Posterior Mean (95% CI)", x = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 20) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "top")
  
```


## Consequences for Person-Specific Estimates

::: {.column width="70%"}

*Rank-order correlations between individual AR estimates*

```{r}
options(knitr.kable.NA = '')
# individual AR effects 
pars = do.call(cbind, lapply(1:length(fits), function(x){
    
    dat = data.frame(
      "AR" = fits[[x]]$person.pars.summary[fits[[x]]$person.pars.summary$Param == "phi(1)_11", "mean"])
    dat[,1] = as.numeric(dat[,1])
    colnames(dat) <- labels[x]
    dat
  }))

tab = round(cor(pars, method = "spearman"),2) 
colnames(tab) <- 1:ncol(pars)
row.names(tab) <- paste0(1:ncol(pars), ". ", rownames(tab))
tab[upper.tri(tab)] <- NA

cap = "Rank-order correlations between individual AR estimates across the different modeling options"

tab %>%
  knitr::kable(., booktabs = TRUE, digits = 2, align = "r",
               ) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_classic() %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 35, position = "float_left")

```

:::


## Consequences for Estimation Times

::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r}
# estimation times 
times = do.call(rbind, lapply(1:length(fits), function(x){
    
    cbind.data.frame(
      "Est. Strategy" = labels[x],
      "Est. Time [min]" = round(max(apply(rstan::get_elapsed_time(fits[[x]]$stanfit),1,sum)) / 60,2),
      "% missing" = round(sum(is.na(fits[[x]]$data$posaff)) / length(fits[[x]]$data$posaff) * 100, 2) 
    )
  }))


knitr::kable(times, booktabs = TRUE) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_classic() %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 30, position = "float_left")

```

:::

. . .

::: {.vspace}
:::

- Using the missing value insertion strategy is computationally costly 
- Ideally, use full `tinterval`-functionality, BUT:
  - Increased estimation times 
  - Can affect model convergence
- In practice, compromise between granularity of recovering the temporal order and estimation performance by limiting the number of consecutive missing values
  - Sensitivity analyses (i.e., different values for `max_NA_seq`)
  - Especially relevant for complex models

- Remove correlation with other random effects (i.e., `ranef_iid` argument)

## Common Issues II


::: {.column width="30%"}
**Factor**
:::

::: {.column width="20%"}
**Impact**
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
**Diagnostics**

:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
**Potential Solution**
:::



::: {.column width="30%"}
Misalignment of parameter priors and variables' scales 
(e.g., visual analogue scales from 0 to 100)
:::

::: {.column width="20%"}
↓ Model convergence

↑ Estimation times 
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
- `mlts_fit()` may print a message, but can be undetected
- Inspect priors in `mlts_model()` object before model estimation
:::

::: {.column width="25%"}
- If possible: consider (re-)scaling the variables close to $N(0,1)$
- More advanced: 
  - Adjust priors
  - BUT: Stan is generally fastest when parameters are in the range of standard normally distributed variables 
:::

## Warning Messages and What to do?

#### Divergent Transitions 

- Can indicate that parameter estimates may not be trustworthy
  - However, false-positives are possible (for more details on this issue, see Gabry et al., 2019)
  - Suggested solution is to run graphical checks
    - For example, parallel co-ordinates plots as shown below

```r
# save flagged MCMC draws
np <- bayesplot::nuts_params(fit$stanfit)

# create plot
bayesplot::mcmc_parcoord(
  fit$posteriors, 
  # for standardized parameters, set:
  transformations = function(x){ (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)},
  np = np, alpha = 0.1) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1))
```

```{r, eval = F}
load("../sections/05-model_extensions/1.1_VAR_2000.Rdata")
np <- bayesplot::nuts_params(fit_VAR_l$stanfit)
bayesplot::mcmc_parcoord(fit_VAR_l$posteriors, 
                         transformations = function(x){ (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)},
                         np = np, alpha = 0.1) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1))
ggsave(filename = "04-practical_aspects/divergent_transistion_illustration.png",
       width = 12, height = 5.5)

```


:::{.references}
Betancourt, M. J. (2017). A Conceptual Introduction to Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (Version 2). *arXiv*. <https://doi.org/10.48550/ARXIV.1701.02434>

Gabry, J., Simpson, D., Vehtari, A., Betancourt, M., & Gelman, A. (2019). Visualization in Bayesian Workflow. *Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A: Statistics in Society, 182(2)*, 389–402. <https://doi.org/10.1111/rssa.12378>


:::
